items.title: Overview
items.text:
# Install on a Linux host with Docker
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- install --start

# Sign in with a Linux account, then list your labs
TOKEN=$(curl -sk https://lab-host:8090/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"alice","password":"..."}' | jq -r .token)
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://lab-host:8090/api/v1/labs

Start the quick start

items.title: over HTTPS
items.text:
One server on your lab host. Every lab, every user, one REST API. Deploy, inspect, exec, capture, and share labs from scripts, CI, or the Containerlab Apps.

Quick start API reference

items.title: One server between your tools and your labs
items.text: Clients sign in with a Linux account and get a token. The server runs each lab for the user who asked, and keeps users' labs apart.

items.title: Everything containerlab does, over the network
items.text: Containerlab is built in as a library. There is no separate CLI to install, and every call runs as the signed-in user's lab.

items.title: Lab lifecycle
items.text:
Deploy from JSON, a file, an archive, or a URL. Redeploy, apply changes, and destroy.

Use the API

items.title: Workspaces
items.text:
Every user gets a lab workspace. Keep topologies in Git repositories and edit them over the API.

Workspaces

items.title: Get in
items.text:
Exec commands, browser terminals, SSH through the server, and node logs, live or static.

Common calls

Stream pcapng from any link, or open Wireshark in the browser.

items.text:
Linux accounts sign in. Users see their own labs, admins see all, and shared labs are open to everyone.

Run labs next to the server, or on a cluster through clabernetes with Kubernetes RBAC.

Install the service

items.text:
One containerlab tools api-server start, or your own docker run. For trials and container-managed hosts.

Run in a container

items.title: Binary
items.text:
Download the binary and supervise it yourself. For debugging and custom setups.

Run the binary

items.title: A lab host in five minutes
items.text: Install the server, add a user, and deploy a lab with curl.

items.title: Build
items.text:
You need Go, Task, and the PAM headers (libpam-dev on Debian and Ubuntu).

git clone https://github.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server.git
cd clab-api-server
task deps                 # libpam-dev, swag, test tools
cp .env.example .env      # set JWT_SECRET
task                      # tidy, generate the OpenAPI spec, build
sudo ./dist/clab-api-server-linux-amd64 -env-file .env
Task Does task build Build dist/clab-api-server-linux-<arch>. task swag Regenerate the OpenAPI spec in docs/ from handler annotations. task test Run the integration tests and write an HTML report to test-reports/. task docs Preview this site. task docs:build Build this site into site/.

items.title: Test
items.text:
The tests in tests_go/ call a running server. Configure them in tests_go/.env (API URL, users, and GOTEST_SIMPLE_TOPOLOGY_CONTENT, a topology with a {lab_name} placeholder), then:

task test                                               # everything
go test -v ./tests_go/... -run TestAuthSuite/TestLoginSuccess   # one test

The test users must exist on the host, in API_USER_GROUP and SUPERUSER_GROUP.

items.title: These docs
items.text:
The site is built with Zensical from docs-site/. You need uv.

task docs          # live preview on http://localhost:8000
task docs:build    # strict build into site/
  • Pages are Markdown in docs-site/; the navigation is in zensical.toml.
  • The API reference is ReDoc reading docs/swagger.json. Run task swag after changing handler annotations.

  • Topology diagrams are clab fences, rendered by the Containerlab topology viewer. Reference a file from docs-site/diagrams/, and its .annotations.json for a fixed layout:

    ```clab file="diagrams/hello.clab.yml" view="split" height="300"
```

  • Every push to main publishes the site to GitHub Pages.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
clab-api-server is a single binary that embeds containerlab as a Go library. It runs on the lab host, signs users in with their Linux accounts, and runs containerlab for them.

Sign-in

Linux user and password, checked through PAM. The server returns a JWT for the following calls.

Labs

Docker or Podman on the same host, or a Kubernetes cluster through clabernetes.

Files

Each user's topologies live in a workspace: ~/.clab/ or $CLAB_LABS_ROOT/<user>/.

items.title: A request, end to end
items.text:
# Diagram only: clients, the API server, and the labs it runs. Not a deployable lab.
name: architecture

topology:
  nodes:
    apps: {kind: linux}
    scripts: {kind: linux}
    ci: {kind: linux}
    api-server: {kind: linux}
    r1: {kind: linux}
    r2: {kind: linux}
    h1: {kind: linux}
    h2: {kind: linux}

  links:
    - endpoints: [r1:eth1, r2:eth1]
    - endpoints: [h1:eth1, h2:eth1]

# Diagram only: clients, the API server, and the labs it runs. Not a deployable lab.
name: architecture
 
topology:
  nodes:
    apps: {kind: linux}
    scripts: {kind: linux}
    ci: {kind: linux}
    api-server: {kind: linux}
    r1: {kind: linux}
    r2: {kind: linux}
    h1: {kind: linux}
    h2: {kind: linux}
 
  links:
    - endpoints: [r1:eth1, r2:eth1]
    - endpoints: [h1:eth1, h2:eth1]
Every client talks HTTPS to one server. The server runs each lab on behalf of the user who owns it.
  1. A client calls POST /login with a Linux user name and password. The server checks them with PAM and checks that the user is in API_USER_GROUP or SUPERUSER_GROUP.
  2. The server answers with a JWT. Every call to /api/v1/* carries it as Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  3. For a lab call, the server resolves the topology in the user's workspace and runs the containerlab operation in-process.
  4. Containers are labelled with their owner. Listing, inspecting, and operating labs only reach labs the user owns, shared labs, or, for superusers, every lab.

items.title: Who sees what
items.text:
User Sees and manages Member of API_USER_GROUP (clab_api) Own labs and shared labs. Member of SUPERUSER_GROUP (clab_admins) Every lab on the host, and the user management endpoints.

With CLAB_RUNTIME=c9s, Kubernetes RBAC decides instead, and the server acts as the user towards the cluster. See Labs on Kubernetes.

items.title: Clients
items.text:
• Containerlab Apps. The VS Code extension, desktop app, and web app sign in to a lab host and use this API for everything.
  • Scripts and CI. Anything that speaks HTTPS and JSON. See Use the API.
  • Interactive docs. A running server serves Swagger UI at /swagger/index.html and ReDoc at /redoc.

Install Security model

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
Install the server on a Linux host with Docker, let one user in, and run a two-node lab with nothing but curl.

This is the lab you will run: two Linux containers, wired together on eth1.

name: hello

topology:
  defaults:
    kind: linux
    image: alpine:3.23
  nodes:
    client: {}
    server: {}
  links:
    - endpoints: [client:eth1, server:eth1]

name: hello
 
topology:
  defaults:
    kind: linux
    image: alpine:3.23
  nodes:
    client: {}
    server: {}
  links:
    - endpoints: [client:eth1, server:eth1]

  1. Install and start the server.

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- install --start

    The server now listens on https://<host>:8090 with a self-signed certificate.

  2. Let a user in. Any Linux account in the clab_api group can sign in with its password.

    sudo usermod -aG clab_api alice

  3. Sign in. The response holds a JWT for every further call.

    API=https://localhost:8090
TOKEN=$(curl -sk -X POST $API/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"alice","password":"..."}' | jq -r .token)

  4. Save the topology. Write the lab above to hello.clab.yml, or download it from the diagram:

    cat > hello.clab.yml <<'EOF'
name: hello

topology:
  defaults:
    kind: linux
    image: alpine:3.23
  nodes:
    client: {}
    server: {}
  links:
    - endpoints: [client:eth1, server:eth1]
EOF

  5. Upload and deploy it. The file goes into your workspace, then the server deploys it from there:

    curl -sk -X PUT "$API/api/v1/labs/workspace/file?path=hello.clab.yml" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --data-binary @hello.clab.yml

curl -sk -X POST "$API/api/v1/labs/hello/deploy?path=hello.clab.yml" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

  6. Look inside. Inspect the lab, then ping across the link from client:

    curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $API/api/v1/labs/hello

curl -sk -X POST "$API/api/v1/labs/hello/exec?nodes=client" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"command": "ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev eth1"}'
curl -sk -X POST "$API/api/v1/labs/hello/exec?nodes=server" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"command": "ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev eth1"}'
curl -sk -X POST "$API/api/v1/labs/hello/exec?nodes=client" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"command": "ping -c 3 10.0.0.2"}'

    Each answer holds the command's stdout, stderr, and exit code per node.

  7. Destroy it.

    curl -sk -X DELETE "$API/api/v1/labs/hello" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

hello.clab.yml stays in Alice's workspace (~/.clab/ by default), ready to deploy again. The Containerlab Apps show the same lab, and can draw, deploy, and open terminals on it.

How it works Use the API Configuration

items.title: Use the API
items.text: Every call except /login and /health needs a token. Sign in once, then send the token as a bearer header.

items.title: Sign in
items.text:
API=https://localhost:8090
TOKEN=$(curl -sk -X POST $API/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"alice","password":"..."}' | jq -r .token)

A token lasts JWT_EXPIRATION (default 24h). Ask for another lifetime at sign-in with sessionDuration:

{"username": "alice", "password": "...", "sessionDuration": "36h"}

The server uses a self-signed certificate unless you configure one, hence -k in these examples.

items.title: Common calls
items.text:
What Call List labs GET /api/v1/labs Deploy from JSON or a URL POST /api/v1/labs with topologyContent or topologySourceUrl Deploy a file from the workspace POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/deploy?path=<file> Deploy an archive POST /api/v1/labs/archive (zip or tar.gz) Inspect a lab GET /api/v1/labs/{lab} Redeploy PUT /api/v1/labs/{lab} Destroy DELETE /api/v1/labs/{lab} (cleanup, purgeLabDir, graceful) Run a command POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/exec (nodes, label filters) Save configs POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/save Node logs GET /api/v1/labs/{lab}/nodes/{node}/logs SSH through the server POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/nodes/{node}/ssh Capture packets GET /api/v1/labs/{lab}/capture/stream?target=<node>:<iface> Events GET /api/v1/events Server status and features GET /health

The full list, with every parameter and response, is in the REST API reference.

items.title: Deploy and inspect
items.text:
curl -sk -X POST $API/api/v1/labs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"topologyContent":{"name":"srl01","topology":{
        "kinds":{"nokia_srlinux":{"type":"ixrd3","image":"ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux"}},
        "nodes":{"srl1":{"kind":"nokia_srlinux"},"srl2":{"kind":"nokia_srlinux"}},
        "links":[{"endpoints":["srl1:e1-1","srl2:e1-1"]}]}}}'

curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $API/api/v1/labs/srl01

items.title: Capture packets
items.text:
Stream a capture to Wireshark on your machine:

curl -sk -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$API/api/v1/labs/srl01/capture/stream?target=srl1:e1-1" | wireshark -k -i -

Repeat target to capture several interfaces into one stream. GET /api/v1/labs/{lab}/capture/interfaces lists what can be captured.

items.title: Follow events
items.text:
/api/v1/events streams container and interface events as NDJSON, one object per line:

curl -sk -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/api/v1/events?initialState=true"

Add interfaceStats=true for interface counters.

items.title: Check what a server supports
items.text:
GET /health needs no token. Its features list names optional capabilities, so clients can hide what an older server or another runtime does not offer:

curl -sk $API/health | jq .features

items.title: Explore interactively
items.text:
A running server documents itself:

https://<host>:8090/swagger/index.html   # Swagger UI, try calls in the browser
https://<host>:8090/redoc                # ReDoc

items.title: Flashpost collection
items.text:
Flashpost is a REST client inside VS Code. The repository ships a ready-made collection for every endpoint in example/flashpost. Import it and set its variables:

Variable Value USER_NAME Linux user to sign in as USER_PASSWORD Its password baseUrl For example localhost:8090

items.title: Timeout
items.text:
Deploy, redeploy, apply, and destroy take an optional timeout: containerlab's --timeout as a Go duration such as 90s, 15m, or 1h, at most 2h.

curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$API/api/v1/labs/demo/deploy?path=demo.clab.yml&timeout=30m"

It applies to POST /api/v1/labs, /api/v1/labs/archive, /api/v1/labs/{lab}/deploy, /apply, PUT /api/v1/labs/{lab}, and DELETE /api/v1/labs/{lab}.

Runtime Default Docker, Podman 5 minutes c9s (Kubernetes) 10 minutes, since clusters pull images and schedule Pods slower

The request itself runs for the timeout plus 5 minutes (a redeploy for twice the timeout plus 5 minutes), so containerlab's own timeout error reaches the client. Servers that take timeout list lab-lifecycle-timeout in /health features.

items.title: Snapshot restore
items.text:
Deploy calls accept restoreAll and restore to start vrnetlab nodes from VM snapshots in the user's workspace.

The server opens each snapshot once, checks it, and places that exact file at $CLAB_RESTORE_STAGING_DIR/<lab>/<node>.tar. Only that file is mounted into the node, so changing the workspace afterwards does not change what the node uses.

Disk space. The staged file is a hard link when the staging folder is on the same filesystem and mount as the workspace, so it costs nothing extra. Otherwise the snapshot is copied. To avoid copies, put CLAB_RESTORE_STAGING_DIR on the same mount as the workspaces, for example /home/.clab-api-restore with the Docker deployment.

Ownership. The folder and every parent must be owned by root and not writable by other users. The server creates missing folders. In a container, mount it at the same path as on the host.

Lifetime. Staged files stay while the lab exists, so node restarts work. The next restore of a node replaces its file. Destroying the lab, or the node with a node filter, through the API removes them.

Snapshots need Docker or Podman; they are not available on c9s.

items.title: Labs on Kubernetes
items.text:
With CLAB_RUNTIME=c9s the API server runs labs on a Kubernetes cluster through clabernetes (c9s) instead of Docker or Podman on its own host. It uses the c9s lab runtime of the containerlab library it links, so labs behave as containerlab deploy -r c9s labs do.

# Diagram only: the API server provisions a namespace per lab and acts as the user. Not a deployable lab.
name: kubernetes

topology:
  nodes:
    alice: {kind: linux}
    bob: {kind: linux}
    api-server: {kind: linux}
    srl1: {kind: linux}
    srl2: {kind: linux}
    ceos1: {kind: linux}
    ceos2: {kind: linux}

  links:
    - endpoints: [srl1:e1-1, srl2:e1-1]
    - endpoints: [ceos1:eth1, ceos2:eth1]

# Diagram only: the API server provisions a namespace per lab and acts as the user. Not a deployable lab.
name: kubernetes
 
topology:
  nodes:
    alice: {kind: linux}
    bob: {kind: linux}
    api-server: {kind: linux}
    srl1: {kind: linux}
    srl2: {kind: linux}
    ceos1: {kind: linux}
    ceos2: {kind: linux}
 
  links:
    - endpoints: [srl1:e1-1, srl2:e1-1]
    - endpoints: [ceos1:eth1, ceos2:eth1]
Each lab gets its own namespace. The server creates it, then acts as the signed-in user, so Kubernetes RBAC decides what each user may do.

In short: Kubernetes RBAC is the authority over labs. The server uses its own identity only to create a namespace for each lab. For everything else it acts as the signed-in user, so a user has the same rights through the server as with kubectl, and the cluster's audit log names them.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Kubernetes 1.31 or later.
  • clabernetes with node run state and the clabwire capture contract (0.11 or later). The server refuses to start against an older clabernetes.
  • Lab namespaces run with the Pod Security level privileged: device containers and the clabwire sidecar are privileged.
  • A default StorageClass that provisions volumes dynamically, unless CLAB_C9S_PERSISTENCE=false.
  • For node stats: the resource metrics API (metrics.k8s.io, e.g. metrics-server).

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Variable Default Meaning CLAB_RUNTIME docker c9s runs labs on Kubernetes. CLAB_KUBECONFIG (empty) Kubeconfig file. Empty uses KUBECONFIG, ~/.kube/config, or in a Pod the ServiceAccount. CLAB_KUBE_CONTEXT (empty) Kubeconfig context; empty uses the current context. CLAB_KUBE_USER_PREFIX clab: Prefix of the Kubernetes user and group names the server acts as, so they cannot collide with the cluster's own users. CLAB_KUBE_NAMESPACE_TEMPLATE c9s-{user}-{lab} Namespace of a user's lab. Needs {user} and {lab}. CLAB_KUBE_LAB_QUOTA (empty) Absolute path of a ResourceQuota manifest (YAML) created in every new lab namespace. CLAB_C9S_EXPOSE_TYPE None Service type of lab nodes: None, ClusterIP, Headless or LoadBalancer. With None, clients reach nodes through the server. CLAB_C9S_PERSISTENCE true Keep node storage (saved configuration) across Pod replacement and a plain destroy. CLAB_C9S_IMAGE_PULL_SECRET (empty) Docker-config Secret the device Pods pull images with, as <namespace>/<name> or a name in the server's own namespace. The server copies it into every lab namespace.

CLAB_KUBE_NAMESPACE cannot be used with c9s: every lab has its own namespace.

items.title: Set up
items.text:
1. Install clabernetes with its lab roles enabled (labRoles.enabled). This ships the ClusterRole clabernetes-lab-editor that lab users get.

  2. Apply the server's RBAC. Adjust clab: in the files if you change CLAB_KUBE_USER_PREFIX.

    kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/docs/kubernetes/provisioner-rbac.yaml \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/docs/kubernetes/admins-rbac.yaml
    • provisioner-rbac.yaml: the ServiceAccount clab-api-server and its ClusterRole clab-api-server-provisioner.
    • admins-rbac.yaml: binds clabernetes-lab-editor to the group clab:admins, so superusers see every lab.

  3. Give the server its identity. Inside the cluster, run it in a Pod with serviceAccountName: clab-api-server. Outside, build a kubeconfig from a token of that ServiceAccount and point CLAB_KUBECONFIG at it:

    kubectl -n clab-api-server create token clab-api-server --duration=8760h

  4. Switch the runtime and restart the server:

    CLAB_RUNTIME=c9s

    On start the server checks its permissions, the clabernetes version, and the lab role, and exits with a clear message if something is missing.

Check a user's rights as the server will use them:

kubectl auth can-i create pods --subresource exec -n c9s-alice-lab1 --as clab:alice --as-group clab:users   # yes
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n c9s-alice-lab1 --as clab:bob --as-group clab:users                           # no

items.title: Users and their rights
items.text:
Linux Kubernetes user alice user clab:alice, group clab:users member of SUPERUSER_GROUP additionally group clab:admins member of the Linux group that owns a shared lab's directory additionally group clab:shared-<group> for that lab

Each lab lives in its own namespace, c9s-<user>-<lab> (or c9s-shared-<lab> for a shared lab). Two users may both have a lab called demo.

items.title: Trust model
items.text:
These roles isolate users from each other: a user can only reach labs in namespaces they are bound in, and every action is attributed to the user in the audit log.

They do not isolate the worker from the lab: lab namespaces are PSA privileged, device containers and the clabwire sidecar run privileged, and RBAC cannot limit pods/exec to one container. Whoever can deploy a lab or exec into it can reach the worker. That is the same trust level as clab_admins on a Docker host. Clusters shared with other workloads should keep labs on dedicated, tainted workers (taints and a nodeSelector in the clabernetes NodeProfile).

items.title: Not supported on c9s
items.text:
These answer 501 with <operation> is not supported by lab runtime c9s:

  • image management (/images)
  • Edgeshark (/tools/edgeshark/*) and Edgeshark's Packetflix URIs (/capture/packetflix); use packet capture instead
  • Wireshark VNC sessions when the server host has no Docker
  • netem, veth, VxLAN and TX offload tools
  • VM snapshots (/snapshots) and deploys that restore them
  • SSHX and GoTTY sharing, fcli, Tailscale status
  • pause and unpause
  • link inspection (/links)
  • host metrics (/health/metrics)

Deploy options that only local runtimes have (node filter, management network overrides, export templates, graceful destroy) also answer 501.

Kubernetes internals

items.title: Shared labs
items.text:
A shared workspace is one folder that every signed-in user works in together. It appears as @shared/ next to each user's own files.

# Diagram only: personal and shared lab folders on one API server.
name: shared-labs

topology:
  nodes:
    alice: {kind: linux}
    bob: {kind: linux}
    api-server: {kind: linux}
    alice-lab: {kind: linux}
    team-lab: {kind: linux}
    bob-lab: {kind: linux}

# Diagram only: personal and shared lab folders on one API server.
name: shared-labs
 
topology:
  nodes:
    alice: {kind: linux}
    bob: {kind: linux}
    api-server: {kind: linux}
    alice-lab: {kind: linux}
    team-lab: {kind: linux}
    bob-lab: {kind: linux}
Alice and Bob each keep their own labs. Both can open, change, and run the labs in the shared folder.

items.title: Turn it on
items.text:
Set a dedicated absolute folder, separate from personal workspaces, and restart the server:

CLAB_SHARED_LABS_ROOT=/var/lib/containerlab/shared-labs

Leave it empty to keep sharing off. A containerized server must mount the folder at the same path inside and outside.

items.title: Who can do what
items.text:
Every API user can read, edit, deploy, operate, and destroy labs in the shared folder. There are no per-user or per-group rules, and users need no extra Linux group memberships. Personal labs keep their usual access rules.

Terminal, SSH, and capture sessions stay private to the user who opened them; superusers keep their usual access.

items.title: Use it
items.text:
Create a directory, upload a topology, and deploy it by its @shared/ path:

curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"path":"@shared/demo"}' \
  $API/api/v1/labs/workspace/directory

curl -sk -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --data-binary @demo.clab.yml \
  "$API/api/v1/labs/workspace/file?path=%40shared%2Fdemo%2Fdemo.clab.yml"

curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$API/api/v1/labs/demo/deploy?path=%40shared%2Fdemo%2Fdemo.clab.yml"

Any other user can now reach /api/v1/labs/demo, its nodes, topology, and events.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Topology listings include shared files as @shared/<dir>/<file>, deployed or not. Keep using that yamlFileName for file and deploy calls.
  • Redeploying or reconfiguring keeps the original owner. To reconfigure, deploy the same shared path with reconfigure=true.
  • Deploys from JSON, an archive, or a URL always create personal labs.
  • Lab names must be unique across all running labs.
  • Destroy keeps the source. purgeLabDir=true also deletes the topology's directory, as long as it is below the shared root; the root itself cannot be purged.
  • Files cannot be moved between personal and shared workspaces.

items.title: Test it
items.text:
With the server configured as above:

GOTEST_SHARED_LABS=true go test -count=1 ./tests_go -run TestSharedLabsSuite

The suite uses tests_go/.env and creates and removes a temporary second API user.

items.title: Topology templates
items.text:
Containerlab renders every topology as a Go template. Files named *.clab.gotmpl are listed like any other topology and take their variables from a file next to them.

File Role lab.clab.gotmpl The template. lab.clab_vars.yml (or .yaml, .json) Its variables, found by name. clab_templates/*.gotmpl Subtemplates.

items.title: Preview
items.text:
Render a template without deploying it:

curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$API/api/v1/labs/lab/topology/rendered?path=repo%2Flabs%2Flab.clab.gotmpl"

The response holds the rendered content, the rendered labName, and the varsFiles that were used. Template errors answer 422.

items.title: Another variables file
items.text:
Pass varsPath, relative to the topology's directory, like containerlab --vars. It works with:

  • GET /api/v1/labs/{lab}/topology/rendered
  • POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/deploy
  • PUT /api/v1/labs/{lab} (redeploy)
  • DELETE /api/v1/labs/{lab} (destroy)

Pass the same varsPath to redeploy and destroy that the lab was deployed with.

items.title: Users and sign-in
items.text: The server has no user database of its own. It signs in Linux accounts on the host with their passwords, and uses Linux groups as roles.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Role Linux group Can User API_USER_GROUP (default clab_api) Work with own labs and shared labs. Superuser SUPERUSER_GROUP (default clab_admins) Work with every lab, and manage users.

Accounts in neither group cannot sign in.

sudo usermod -aG clab_api alice
sudo usermod -aG clab_admins bob

Superuser rights follow the group on every request. Taking someone out of clab_api stops new sign-ins; tokens they already have work until they expire.

items.title: Sign in
items.text:
POST /login takes a user name and password, checks them with PAM (the login service), and returns a JWT:

curl -sk -X POST https://localhost:8090/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"alice","password":"..."}'

Tokens are signed with JWT_SECRET and expire after JWT_EXPIRATION, or after sessionDuration if the request sets it. Changing JWT_SECRET signs everyone out.

items.title: Manage users over the API
items.text: Superusers can manage Linux accounts through /api/v1/users: list, create, update, and delete them, and set their groups. Every user can read and update their own account, and change their own password with PUT /api/v1/users/{username}/password.

items.title: Where a user's labs live
items.text: Each user has a workspace: ~/.clab/ by default, or $CLAB_LABS_ROOT/<username>/ when CLAB_LABS_ROOT is set. Files in it belong to the user. See Workspaces and topology files.

items.title: Workspaces and topology files
items.text:
A user's workspace holds their topologies, annotations, and any other lab files. Keep several labs, or whole Git repositories, side by side.

The workspace is ~/.clab/, or $CLAB_LABS_ROOT/<username>/ when that is set. Shared labs appear in it as @shared/.

items.title: Discovery
items.text:
GET /api/v1/labs/topology/files lists every topology in the workspace, in nested directories too:

  • *.clab.yml, *.clab.yaml, and *.clab.gotmpl (templates) are topologies.
  • Hidden files and directories (including .git), node_modules, __pycache__, symbolic links, and runtime directories with .state.clab.yaml or topology-data.json are skipped.
  • Repositories named clab-* are still found.

Two files in a repository show up as two entries:

{
  "labName": "topology1",
  "yamlFileName": "repo/labs/topology1.clab.yaml",
  "annotationsFileName": "repo/labs/topology1.clab.yaml.annotations.json",
  "hasAnnotations": false,
  "deploymentState": "undeployed",
  "absolutePath": "/home/alice/.clab/repo/labs/topology1.clab.yaml"
}

The lab name is the YAML name, or the file name if there is none. __gitBranch__ and __gitHash__ in a name expand as containerlab does.

items.title: Address a file by its path
items.text:
yamlFileName is relative to the workspace root and identifies the document, even when two repositories use the same file name. Pass it as path:

curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$API/api/v1/labs/topology1/deploy?path=repo%2Flabs%2Ftopology1.clab.yaml"

Lab names still have to be distinct to run labs at the same time.

To tell which file a running lab came from, compare absolutePath with absLabPath in inspect output and lab-path in events.

items.title: Endpoints
items.text:
Call Purpose GET /api/v1/labs/topology/files List topologies. GET\|PUT /api/v1/labs/{lab}/topology/yaml Read or write the topology of a running lab, or the canonical <lab>.clab.yml of an undeployed one. GET\|PUT /api/v1/labs/{lab}/topology/annotations Read or write its annotations. GET\|PUT\|DELETE\|HEAD /api/v1/labs/{lab}/topology/file?path=… Work with one file by the path from the listing. POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/topology/file/rename Rename a file. POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/deploy?path=… Deploy a file from the workspace. GET /api/v1/labs/{lab}/topology/rendered?path=… Render a template without deploying it. GET /api/v1/labs/workspace/tree The whole workspace as a tree. GET\|PUT\|DELETE /api/v1/labs/workspace/file?path=… Any file in the workspace. POST /api/v1/labs/workspace/directory Create a directory. GET /api/v1/labs/workspace/events Stream changes to workspace files.

Older flat and one-directory-per-lab workspaces keep their lab names, and lab-relative file paths keep working. An explicit workspace path wins when its first directory exists in the workspace.

items.title: Browser clients
items.text:
Browser apps on another origin need to be allowed:

CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://localhost:5173,https://ui.example.com

The Containerlab web and desktop apps do not need this.

items.title: Install
items.text: The server runs on Linux, amd64 or arm64. Containerlab is built in, so there is no separate containerlab binary to install.

items.title: Requirements
items.text: Requirement Notes Linux Any modern distribution. Container runtime Docker (default) or Podman on the host, or a Kubernetes cluster with clabernetes. PAM The default login PAM service. Nothing to configure on most distributions. Groups Users who sign in must be in clab_api or clab_admins. The installer creates both.

items.title: Choose a method
items.text:
Method Best for You manage Systemd service Lab hosts you keep, backends for the Containerlab Apps Nothing beyond the config file. Recommended. containerlab tools api-server Trials, demos, temporary access Nothing; it pulls and starts a container. docker run Hosts where everything runs in containers Mounts, config, and lifecycle. Binary Debugging, custom supervision Config and process lifetime.

All methods listen on HTTPS port 8090 by default.

Systemd service

items.title: Binary
items.text:
Download only the binary for the host's architecture, and run it the way you want.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- pull-only

This installs /usr/local/bin/clab-api-server and nothing else. Start it with an env file:

sudo clab-api-server -env-file /path/to/clab-api-server.env

Start from .env.example and change at least JWT_SECRET. Every setting can also be an environment variable; see the configuration reference.

Note

Run it as root, like the service does. With a direct sudo run, keep proxy variables with sudo -E.

The groups in API_USER_GROUP and SUPERUSER_GROUP must exist:

sudo groupadd -f clab_api
sudo groupadd -f clab_admins

items.title: Container
items.text: The server image is ghcr.io/srl-labs/clab-api-server/clab-api-server. Containerlab can start it for you, or you run it yourself.

items.title: containerlab tools
items.text:
The quickest way to try the server. Containerlab pulls the image, creates the container, and configures it:

sudo containerlab tools api-server start
sudo containerlab tools api-server status
sudo containerlab tools api-server stop

Common flags of start:

Flag Default Meaning --port, -p 8090 Port the API is exposed on. --host localhost Host address of the API server. --labs-dir, -l Directory mounted as the labs root. --jwt-secret random Secret that signs session tokens. --tls-enable true Serve HTTPS.

items.title: docker run
items.text:
For hosts where you manage containers yourself. The server needs the host's container runtime, network namespaces, Linux accounts, and home directories:

docker run -d \
  --name clab-api-server \
  --privileged \
  --network host \
  --pid host \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v /var/run/netns:/var/run/netns \
  -v /var/lib/docker/containers:/var/lib/docker/containers \
  -v /etc/passwd:/etc/passwd:ro \
  -v /etc/shadow:/etc/shadow:ro \
  -v /etc/group:/etc/group:ro \
  -v /etc/gshadow:/etc/gshadow:ro \
  -v /home:/home \
  -v /var/lib/clab-api-server:/var/lib/clab-api-server \
  ghcr.io/srl-labs/clab-api-server/clab-api-server:latest
Mount or flag Why Docker socket, /var/lib/docker/containers Manage lab containers and read their logs. /var/run/netns, --network host, --privileged Wire links and run network tools. /etc/passwd, shadow, group, gshadow Sign users in with PAM and check their groups. /home Users' workspaces (~/.clab/). --pid host Keep the host's /etc/hosts entries for lab nodes up to date.

Pass settings with -e, for example -e LOG_LEVEL=debug. See the configuration reference.

items.title: Paths that must match
items.text:
Paths the server hands to containerlab must be the same inside and outside the container. To use another labs root, set the variable and mount it at the same path:

  -e CLAB_LABS_ROOT=/var/lib/containerlab/labs \
  -v /var/lib/containerlab/labs:/var/lib/containerlab/labs \

The same applies to CLAB_SHARED_LABS_ROOT and CLAB_RESTORE_STAGING_DIR.

items.title: Systemd service
items.text:
The installer picks the right binary for the host, writes a config file, creates the user groups, and installs a systemd unit.

  1. Run the installer.

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- install

    It creates:

    • /usr/local/bin/clab-api-server
    • /etc/clab-api-server/clab-api-server.env, with a random JWT_SECRET
    • /etc/systemd/system/clab-api-server.service
    • the groups clab_api and clab_admins, if missing

  2. Review the config. At least set API_SERVER_HOST to the name or address clients use to reach this host.

    sudoedit /etc/clab-api-server/clab-api-server.env

    All settings are listed in the configuration reference.

  3. Let users in.

    sudo usermod -aG clab_api alice      # own labs
sudo usermod -aG clab_admins bob     # every lab

  4. Start the service.

    sudo systemctl enable --now clab-api-server
sudo systemctl status clab-api-server

Tip

install --start enables and starts the service right away with the generated defaults. Restart it after you edit the config file.

The service runs as root: it controls the container runtime, network namespaces, Linux users, and lab files.

items.title: Behind a proxy
items.text:
Export the proxy variables and keep them for the installer with sudo -E:

export HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080
export HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/install.sh | sudo -E bash -s -- install

The service needs them too: add HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and NO_PROXY to /etc/clab-api-server/clab-api-server.env and restart it.

items.title: Store labs outside home directories
items.text:
By default each user's topologies live in ~/.clab/. To keep them elsewhere, set an absolute path:

CLAB_LABS_ROOT=/var/lib/containerlab/labs

Files then go to /var/lib/containerlab/labs/<username>/. ~ is not expanded, because the service runs as root on behalf of many users.

Quick start Upgrade and remove

items.title: Upgrade
items.text:
Check for a newer release and upgrade the installed binary in place:

clab-api-server version check
sudo clab-api-server version upgrade

The installer can do the same, and also install a specific release. Installing an older tag is the supported way to downgrade:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- upgrade
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- upgrade --version clab-0.73.0-api-0.2.1

An upgrade restarts the service only if it was running before. Release tags are listed on the releases page.

items.title: Uninstall
items.text:
Remove the service and binary, and keep the config file:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srl-labs/clab-api-server/main/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- uninstall

Add --purge to remove the config too, and --yes to skip the prompt.

Uninstalling leaves labs, workspaces, and the clab_api and clab_admins groups in place.

items.title: REST API
items.text:
Every endpoint, parameter, and response, generated from the server's source with each release.

Open the API reference OpenAPI JSON OpenAPI YAML

items.title: Areas
items.text: Path What it covers POST /login Sign in with a Linux account; returns a JWT. GET /health Status, version, runtime, and features. No token needed. /api/v1/labs Deploy, inspect, redeploy, apply, validate, and destroy labs. Exec, save, logs, stats, interfaces, graphs. /api/v1/labs/{lab}/nodes/{node} One node: start, stop, restart, logs, SSH, browser terminals, and proxied web ports. /api/v1/labs/{lab}/capture Packet capture streams and Wireshark sessions. /api/v1/labs/workspace, …/topology Files in the user's workspace. See workspaces. /api/v1/events Live container and interface events (NDJSON). /api/v1/terminal-sessions, /api/v1/ssh Open terminal and SSH sessions. /api/v1/tools Certificates, netem, veth, VxLAN, Edgeshark. /api/v1/images Container images on the host. /api/v1/users Linux user management. /api/v1/version Server version and update check.

items.title: On a running server
items.text:
The same reference, matching that server's version:

https://<host>:8090/swagger/index.html   # Swagger UI, try calls with your token
https://<host>:8090/redoc                # ReDoc

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
The server reads settings from environment variables, or from an env file passed with -env-file. The systemd install uses /etc/clab-api-server/clab-api-server.env; restart the service after a change.

Start from .env.example.

items.title: Server
items.text: Variable Default What it does API_PORT 8090 Listen port. API_SERVER_HOST localhost (installer) Host name or IP clients use to reach this host, for example in SSH access details. LOG_LEVEL info debug, info, warn, or error. GIN_MODE release (installer) Web framework mode: debug or release. TRUSTED_PROXIES empty Reverse proxies whose forwarded headers are trusted: comma-separated IPs, nil for none, empty for all. CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS empty Comma-separated browser origins allowed to call the API directly.

items.title: TLS
items.text: Variable Default What it does TLS_ENABLE true Serve HTTPS. TLS_AUTO_CERT true Create and reuse a self-signed certificate when no certificate files are set. TLS_CERT_FILE empty Your certificate. TLS_KEY_FILE empty Its private key.

items.title: Sign-in
items.text: Variable Default What it does JWT_SECRET random (installer) Signs session tokens. Keep it secret; changing it signs everyone out. JWT_EXPIRATION 24h Token lifetime, for example 24h or 7d. API_USER_GROUP clab_api Linux group that may sign in. SUPERUSER_GROUP clab_admins Linux group that sees and manages every lab and user.

items.title: Labs and files
items.text: Variable Default What it does CLAB_RUNTIME docker docker, podman, or c9s for Kubernetes. CLAB_LABS_ROOT empty Absolute root for workspaces: $CLAB_LABS_ROOT/<user>/. Empty uses ~/.clab/. CLAB_SHARED_LABS_ROOT empty Absolute folder for shared labs. Empty turns them off. CLAB_HOSTS_FILE empty Host-visible hosts file to keep lab entries in. In a container with --pid host, /proc/1/root/etc/hosts is found automatically. CLAB_RESTORE_STAGING_DIR /var/lib/clab-api-server/restore Where snapshot restores are staged.

items.title: Terminals, SSH, and scripts
items.text: Variable Default What it does SSH_BASE_PORT 2223 First port for SSH access through the server. SSH_MAX_PORT 2322 Last port for SSH access. TERMINAL_MAX_SESSIONS_PER_USER 128 Open browser terminals per user. TERMINAL_IDLE_TIMEOUT 30m How long a resumable terminal keeps running after its last client left. Other terminals end with their client. API_HOST_SCRIPTS false Let script buttons run shell scripts on this host, each as the signed-in Linux user. Accounts with a nologin or false shell are refused. No effect on c9s.

items.title: Packet capture
items.text: Variable Default What it does CAPTURE_WIRESHARK_DOCKER_IMAGE ghcr.io/srl-labs/wireshark-vnc-docker:latest Image of Wireshark-in-the-browser sessions. CAPTURE_WIRESHARK_PULL_POLICY always always, missing, or never. CAPTURE_WIRESHARK_SESSION_TTL 2h Lifetime of a Wireshark session. CAPTURE_PACKETFLIX_PORT 5001 Edgeshark packetflix port (Docker and Podman). CAPTURE_REMOTE_HOSTNAME empty Host name put into Edgeshark capture links. CAPTURE_EDGESHARK_EXTRA_ENV_VARS empty Extra environment variables for Edgeshark, for example proxy settings.

items.title: Fabric checks (fcling)
items.text:
Docker and Podman only.

Variable Default What it does FCLING_DOCKER_IMAGE ghcr.io/srl-labs/fcling:0.9.0 Image of fcling reports and each lab's fabric engine. FCLING_PULL_POLICY missing always, missing, or never. FCLING_GNMI_PORT 57400 gNMI port for nodes of labs without their own. Set one per lab with gnmiPort on POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/fcling/engine. FCLING_STATE_DIR /var/lib/clab-api-server/fcling Where each lab's chosen gNMI port is kept.

items.title: Kubernetes (c9s)
items.text:
Only with CLAB_RUNTIME=c9s. See Labs on Kubernetes for details.

Variable Default What it does CLAB_KUBECONFIG empty Kubeconfig file. Empty uses KUBECONFIG, ~/.kube/config, or the Pod's ServiceAccount. CLAB_KUBE_CONTEXT empty Kubeconfig context. CLAB_KUBE_USER_PREFIX clab: Prefix of the Kubernetes users and groups the server acts as. CLAB_KUBE_NAMESPACE_TEMPLATE c9s-{user}-{lab} Namespace of a user's lab. CLAB_KUBE_LAB_QUOTA empty ResourceQuota manifest created in every lab namespace. CLAB_C9S_EXPOSE_TYPE None Service type of lab nodes: None, ClusterIP, Headless, or LoadBalancer. CLAB_C9S_PERSISTENCE true Keep node storage across Pod replacement and a plain destroy. CLAB_C9S_IMAGE_PULL_SECRET empty Image pull secret copied into every lab namespace.

items.title: What topologies can read
items.text: After loading its settings, the server removes them (every variable on this page except CLAB_RUNTIME) from its own environment, so ${VAR} in a topology cannot read them. Other variables, such as proxy settings, DOCKER_*, and containerlab's own CLAB_* options, stay visible to containerlab and to topologies. Do not keep secrets in them.

items.title: Kubernetes internals
items.text: The details behind Labs on Kubernetes: what the server creates, whose identity each call uses, what clients see, and how nodes are reached.

items.title: Users and their rights
items.text:
Provisioning (the server's identity). On the first deploy of a lab the server creates its namespace (c9s-<user>-<lab>, or c9s-shared-<lab> for a topology under @shared/) with the labels containerlab.dev/runtime=clabernetes, clab-owner=<user>, clab-lab=<lab>, app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=clab-api-server and pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged, and in it:

  • a RoleBinding of clabernetes-lab-editor to clab:<user> (or the group clab:shared-<group>); the role also grants get on the namespace object, which containerlab reads before it deploys into it, and bound in the namespace that is the lab's namespace only,
  • the ResourceQuota from CLAB_KUBE_LAB_QUOTA, and a copy of the image pull secret, if set.

Lab calls (the user's identity). Deploy, apply, destroy, inspect, exec, save, start/stop/restart, events, logs, terminals, port-forwards and stats run through the containerlab library as the user, with Kubernetes impersonation. The cluster's audit log names the user, and a user has the same rights through the server as with kubectl.

Listing. The server lists the namespaces labelled clab-owner=<user> (and the shared ones of the user's groups) with its own identity, then inspects each as the user. Superusers inspect every namespace as clab:admins. The events stream watches each of the user's lab namespaces as the user.

Destroy. A plain destroy keeps the node storage (the saved configuration) and therefore the namespace; the next deploy reuses both. The server deletes the namespace once containerlab removed the lab and no claims are left, and always on cleanup=true. It only deletes namespaces it created.

Names. Lab names are unique per user, not per server: two users may both have a lab demo. A superuser addressing a lab name that several other users have gets 409.

The server's own checks (clab-owner, superuser, shared workspace) stay in place, so a request fails closed if either the server or Kubernetes refuses it.

What users can edit. The lab editor role lets users update their Topology, which carries the lab's clab-owner label and the topology file containerlab deployed from (annotation containerlab.dev/topo-file). The server reads, applies and purges that file, so it does not take either from the Topology: a lab's owner is the one of its namespace, and its topology file (labPath/absLabPath in inspect) is kept only when it lies in the owner's workspace, or for a shared lab in the shared workspace under a directory of the lab's group. Otherwise inspect reports k8s://<namespace>/topologies/<lab>, as for a lab without a recorded file, and file operations that need the topology answer 404. The events stream corrects the clab-owner and clab-topo-file attributes of container events the same way, so they always match inspect; an event whose records the server cannot check (the cluster does not answer) is left out.

The server's own ClusterRole, clab-api-server-provisioner:

Resource Verbs Why namespaces create, delete, get, list lab namespaces rolebindings create, get bind the lab's users clusterroles clabernetes-lab-editor bind, get only this role can be handed out; get for the startup check users impersonate act as the user; resourceNames cannot match a prefix, so users are not limited (list every clab:<user> to limit them) groups clab:users, clab:admins impersonate add clab:shared-<group> for every group that owns shared labs resourcequotas create CLAB_KUBE_LAB_QUOTA secrets create (and get on the source secret) copy CLAB_C9S_IMAGE_PULL_SECRET

It has no rights on clabernetes resources or Pods itself. The server can impersonate any user name, so treat its credentials like a cluster administrator's.

items.title: Startup checks
items.text:
Before it serves requests the server:

  1. runs a SelfSubjectAccessReview for every permission of clab-api-server-provisioner and lists every one that is denied,
  2. runs containerlab's clabernetes release check: the published OpenAPI schema of nodes.c9s.run must have spec.runState (any authenticated identity may read it), and
  3. checks that the ClusterRole clabernetes-lab-editor exists.

If any of them fails, it exits with a message that names what is missing.

items.title: What clients see
items.text:
GET /health reports the runtime:

{
  "status": "healthy",
  "runtime": "c9s",
  "namespaceMode": "per-lab",
  "features": ["validate", "graph-mermaid", "graph-dot", "exec-filters", "lab-lifecycle-node-filter",
               "save-copy", "inspect-details", "node-stats", "log-stream", "terminal-resume",
               "node-logs-runtime", "interface-state", "c9s-runtime", "lab-host-info",
               "capture-stream", "wireshark-vnc", "lab-lifecycle-timeout"]
}
Feature Meaning c9s-runtime Labs run on Kubernetes through clabernetes. Only with CLAB_RUNTIME=c9s. node-logs-runtime Node logs come from the configured runtime (on c9s: the device container log). interface-state The events stream reports the state of node interfaces (create, update, delete with state up, down, lower-layer-down, ...), as netlink does for Docker labs. node-stats Left out on c9s while metrics.k8s.io is not served. lab-host-info GET /api/v1/lab-host describes the lab runtime (all runtimes). capture-stream Packet capture through clabwire: capture/interfaces and capture/stream (see Packet capture). Only with CLAB_RUNTIME=c9s. wireshark-vnc Wireshark VNC capture sessions. On c9s only while Docker answers on the server host (checked once a minute). lab-lifecycle-timeout Deploy, redeploy, apply and destroy take timeout (see Timeouts). With every runtime.

namespaceMode is always per-lab: every lab has its own namespace.

GET /api/v1/lab-host (any signed-in user) names the cluster and the deploy defaults the user's labs get:

{
  "runtime": "c9s",
  "defaultTimeout": "10m",
  "capture": {
    "wiresharkVnc": false,
    "wiresharkImage": "ghcr.io/srl-labs/wireshark-vnc-docker:latest",
    "wiresharkPullPolicy": "always"
  },
  "c9s": {
    "context": "c9s-provisioner",
    "cluster": "c9s",
    "namespacePattern": "c9s-alice-{lab}",
    "sharedNamespacePattern": "c9s-shared-{lab}",
    "exposeType": "None",
    "persistence": true,
    "imagePullSecret": "regcred",
    "labQuota": false,
    "noTopologyCR": false,
    "metrics": true
  }
}

context and cluster are names from the server's kubeconfig ("" and in-cluster with the Pod's ServiceAccount); the cluster's address, credentials and file paths are never reported. namespacePattern is CLAB_KUBE_NAMESPACE_TEMPLATE rendered for the signed-in user with {lab} left in, imagePullSecret the secret's name without its namespace, labQuota whether CLAB_KUBE_LAB_QUOTA is set, and metrics whether metrics.k8s.io is served. noTopologyCR is always false: the server deploys every lab with clabernetes' Topology resource, which carries the lab's owner and topology file. defaultTimeout is containerlab's timeout of a deploy, redeploy, apply or destroy that passes no timeout (see Timeouts).

capture describes packet capture with every runtime, with the defaults applied: wiresharkVnc whether the server runs Wireshark VNC sessions for the user's labs (on c9s while Docker answers on the server host, as wireshark-vnc in /health), wiresharkImage and wiresharkPullPolicy their image and when it is pulled (CAPTURE_WIRESHARK_DOCKER_IMAGE, CAPTURE_WIRESHARK_PULL_POLICY: always, missing or never). Docker and Podman servers answer without c9s and add Edgeshark, which runs next to their labs: its packetflix port (CAPTURE_PACKETFLIX_PORT) and the names of the variables in CAPTURE_EDGESHARK_EXTRA_ENV_VARS, never their values:

{
  "runtime": "docker",
  "defaultTimeout": "5m",
  "capture": {
    "wiresharkVnc": true,
    "wiresharkImage": "ghcr.io/srl-labs/wireshark-vnc-docker:latest",
    "wiresharkPullPolicy": "always",
    "edgeshark": { "packetflixPort": 5001, "extraEnvVars": ["HTTP_PROXY", "NO_PROXY"] }
  }
}

Features that need Docker or Podman on the server host are left out on c9s: snapshot-save, deploy-restore, sshx-readers, gotty-options.

Inspect records of c9s nodes carry namespace, pod, container, node_uid, exposed_ports and load_balancer_address; container_id is <namespace>/<lab>/<node> and the node name is <lab>-<node>. Otherwise they read like Docker's:

  • state is created, running or exited, and status Created, health: starting, healthy or Exited;
  • labPath/absLabPath is the topology file on the server host the lab was deployed from (see What users can edit for when the server reports k8s://<namespace>/topologies/<lab> instead).

The events stream is containerlab's: container events with Docker's actions (create, start, kill, stop, die, destroy, health_status: ...) and attributes (containerlab, clab-node-name, clab-node-kind, clab-owner, clab-topo-file, image, mgmt_ipv4, state, ...), plus namespace, node and pod; interface events for the node's link interfaces under their topology names, eth0 and lo. A user's stream covers the namespaces of the user's labs; a superuser's every namespace.

items.title: How the server reaches nodes
items.text:
Path On c9s Deploy, apply, destroy, inspect, start/stop/restart, exec, save, validate, events containerlab's c9s runtime. Apply is a deploy; dryRun=true returns the plan as runtimePlan. Node logs The device container log (tail, follow, timestamps). Terminals shell and telnet exec in the device container; ssh logs in with the server's SSH client over a port-forward to port 22, or to the LoadBalancer address when the node exposes port 22. SSH access (/nodes/{node}/ssh) The server's port range as before; every connection is a port-forward to the node's port 22. Browser ports The node's exposed ports, each with a proxyPath: ANY /api/v1/labs/{lab}/nodes/{node}/ports/{port}/proxy/* proxies HTTP and WebSockets through a port-forward. The Authorization header is not forwarded. Stats metrics.k8s.io (CPU over the metrics window, memory working set of the device containers). Without the API the stats stream answers 501. Packet capture containerlab's c9s capture: clabwire in the node's pod, one merged pcapng stream. See Packet capture. Interfaces (/interfaces) containerlab's c9s interface inspection as the user: per running node (<lab>-<node>) the lab link interfaces with their aliases, eth0 and lo, with MAC, index, MTU, type and state, the interfaces the events stream reports. Graphs Rendered from the topology file, without the cluster.

Lab names must be lowercase DNS labels (letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter). Other names are refused with the name to use instead.

items.title: Timeouts
items.text: On c9s containerlab waits up to 10 minutes by default for a lab's Pods, as containerlab deploy -r c9s does: a cluster pulls node images and schedules Pods slower than a local Docker. Deploy, redeploy, apply and destroy take an optional timeout query parameter (containerlab's --timeout, a Go duration such as 30m, at most 2h) for labs with large images. The request runs for the timeout plus 5 minutes, and a redeploy for twice the timeout plus 5 minutes, so containerlab's own timeout error reaches the client.

items.title: Packet capture
items.text:
On c9s the server captures through containerlab's c9s capture: clabwire, the sidecar in every lab pod, captures the requested lab link interfaces, and containerlab merges them into one pcapng section. Every call runs as the signed-in user, so Kubernetes decides whether the user may capture (pods/exec on the lab's pods, which clabernetes-lab-editor grants). Edgeshark is not used: clabwire only allows the interfaces of the lab's links, so the management interface and c9s0 cannot be captured.

The stream has one interface per target, named <node>:<interface>, before any packet, and packets in timestamp order. Captures longer than clabwire's one-hour limit are chained by containerlab without gaps or duplicates. When the client goes away the capture stops in the pod (clabwire ends on stdin close).

items.title: List capturable interfaces
items.text:
GET /api/v1/labs/{lab}/capture/interfaces

Returns the lab link interfaces of the running nodes, with the far end of each link:

[
  {
    "node": "srl1",
    "interface": "e1-1",
    "alias": "ethernet-1/1",
    "peerNode": "srl2",
    "peerInterface": "e1-1"
  }
]

alias appears only when the interface has one.

items.title: Stream a capture
items.text:
GET /api/v1/labs/{lab}/capture/stream?target=<node>:<interface>

Returns application/x-pcapng, chunked and flushed as packets arrive. The stream runs until the duration or packet limit is reached, or the client disconnects.

Parameter Meaning target <node>:<interface> to capture. Repeat it for several interfaces in one stream. Required. duration Stop after this long, as a Go duration such as 30s. Default: until the client disconnects. packetLimit Stop after this many packets across all targets. snapLength Bytes kept per packet, 64 to 1048576. Default 262144. download 1 adds Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="<lab>-<timestamp>.pcapng".

Errors before the first byte are JSON; later ones end the stream.

Status When 400 A target the lab cannot capture, or an invalid duration or limit. 403 Kubernetes refuses the user. 404 The user has no lab of that name. 409 A target node is not running.

A target names the node as the topology does (or its sanitized name) and the interface by name or alias, e.g. srl1:ethernet-1/1. The node ends at the first colon.

Wireshark VNC. POST /api/v1/labs/{lab}/capture/wireshark-vnc-sessions takes the node's inspect name (<lab>-<node>) as containerName and an interface (or alias) as interfaceName, and starts one Wireshark VNC container per node on the server host. The server captures the node's requested interfaces as the signed-in user, in one pcapng stream like capture/stream, and writes it into a named pipe in the container (docker exec -i), which the container's Wireshark reads. The container is not attached to an Edgeshark network and does not reach the server. This needs Docker on the server host; without it the routes answer 501 and /health leaves out wireshark-vnc.

The pipe is the CLABWIRE_CAPTURE_PIPE mode of wireshark-vnc-docker, so CAPTURE_WIRESHARK_DOCKER_IMAGE (default ghcr.io/srl-labs/wireshark-vnc-docker:latest) must be an image that has it; the current :latest does. With an older image no pipe appears, and the session fails within a minute (see below).

Stopping and restarting the capture inside the session's Wireshark works: each time Wireshark opens the pipe, the server starts a new capture into it, and stops it when Wireshark closes the pipe. Closing the session, or its expiry (CAPTURE_WIRESHARK_SESSION_TTL), stops the capture in the pods and the container. When the capture fails (for example when the node's pod is gone, or the lab was destroyed), the server stops the session's container and its ready and vnc routes answer 500 with the reason until the session is closed or expires.

items.title: Security model
items.text:
The server runs as root and acts on behalf of Linux users. These are the rules that keep users apart.

Topic How it works Server process Runs as root, since it controls the container runtime, network namespaces, Linux users, and lab files. Containerlab runs inside it as a library, not as a separate command. Sign-in Linux credentials checked by PAM. Only members of API_USER_GROUP or SUPERUSER_GROUP get a token. Sessions JWTs signed with JWT_SECRET, valid for JWT_EXPIRATION. Ownership Containers carry their owner as a label. Users reach their own labs and shared labs; superusers reach all. Files Each user's workspace belongs to that user. Paths are checked to stay inside the workspace or the shared folder. SSH access A port from SSH_BASE_PORT–SSH_MAX_PORT forwards to the node's port 22 and expires automatically. Transport HTTPS by default, with a self-signed certificate until you provide one. Topology variables The server's own settings are removed from its environment, so topologies cannot read JWT_SECRET and friends. See configuration. Kubernetes With c9s, the server acts as the user towards the cluster, and Kubernetes RBAC decides. See trust model.

items.title: Recommendations
items.text:
• Keep JWT_SECRET long and random. The installer generates one.
  • Use your own certificate with TLS_CERT_FILE and TLS_KEY_FILE for hosts others reach.
  • Put only trusted people in clab_admins: they see and operate every lab and manage Linux users.
  • Leave API_HOST_SCRIPTS off unless users should run scripts on the host as themselves.
  • Treat a lab host as shared infrastructure: anyone who can deploy a privileged lab node can reach the host through it.
